articles.title: Accelerated Zeckendorf Game: Conjecture 1.7 implies Conjecture 1.6
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci
numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Suppose that for every $n$ such that
the state consisting of $n$ copies of $F_1$ is losing, and every $k$ with $3k \le n$, the state
consisting of $k$ copies of $F_3$ and $n - 3k$ copies of $F_1$ is losing. Then for every $n > 9$
the state consisting of $n$ copies of $F_1$ (the starting position of the Accelerated Zeckendorf
Game on $n$) is winning.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Theorem 1.8 (with Conjectures 1.6 and 1.7).

articles.title: Accelerated Zeckendorf Game: Conjecture 1.7 in its first five cases
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci
numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Let $n$ be such that the state
consisting of $n$ copies of $F_1$ (the starting position of the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on
$n$) is losing. Then for every $k$ with $1 \le k \le 5$ and $3k \le n$, the state consisting of
$k$ copies of $F_3$ and $n - 3k$ copies of $F_1$ is losing.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Lemma 1.9.

articles.title: Lower bound on the length of an Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci numbers
as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Let $n \ge 1$ and let $F_k$ be the largest
Fibonacci number with $F_k \le n$, the largest term of the Zeckendorf decomposition of $n$. Then
every complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $n$ (a sequence of moves from $n$ copies of $F_1$
to a state from which no move is possible) has at least $k - 1$ moves.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Lemma 2.1.

articles.title: Sharp lower bound for the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on a Fibonacci number
articles.statement:
Index the
Fibonacci numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$, and let $k \ge 1$. Every
complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $F_k$ (a sequence of moves from $F_k$ copies of $F_1$ to
a state from which no move is possible) has at least $k - 1$ moves, and some complete game on
$F_k$ has exactly $k - 1$ moves.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Lemma 2.3.

articles.title: Sharp lower bound on the length of an Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci
numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Let $n \ge 1$ and let $F_k$ be the
largest Fibonacci number with $F_k \le n$, the largest term of the Zeckendorf decomposition of
$n$. Then every complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $n$ (a sequence of moves from $n$ copies
of $F_1$ to a state from which no move is possible) has at least $k - 1$ moves, and some complete
game on $n$ has exactly $k - 1$ moves.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Theorem 1.4.

articles.title: The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game terminates at the Zeckendorf decomposition
articles.statement:
Index the
Fibonacci numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Let $n$ be a natural
number, let $Z(n)$ be the number of terms of the Zeckendorf decomposition of $n$, and let $IZ(n)$
be the sum of the indices $k$ of its terms $F_k$. Then there is no infinite sequence of moves
starting from $n$ copies of $F_1$. Moreover, every complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $n$
(a sequence of moves from $n$ copies of $F_1$ to a state from which no move is possible) ends at
the state with one copy of each term of the Zeckendorf decomposition of $n$, and its number $L$
of moves satisfies

$$L \le \frac{3 + \sqrt 5}{2} n - IZ(n) - \frac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2} Z(n).$$

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Theorem 1.3.

articles.title: Terminal states are losing in the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Every state of the
Accelerated Zeckendorf Game from which no move is possible is a losing state.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 2.2, rule (1).

articles.title: Losing states of the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
The losing and the winning states of
the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game are defined by simultaneous induction: a state is losing when
every move from it leads to a winning state, and a state is winning when some move from it leads
to a losing state. In particular every state from which no move is possible is losing.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 2.2 (rules (1)-(4) for winning and losing states).

articles.title: Moving a Fibonacci number of pairs in the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Index the
Fibonacci numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{j+1} = F_j + F_{j-1}$, extended by $F_0 = 1$ and
$F_{-1} = 0$. Let $p \ge 2$ and $i \ge 1$, and let $s$ be a state with $F_{i-1}$ copies of
$F_{p-1}$, $F_i$ copies of $F_p$ and no copy of $F_{p+1}$. Let $t$ be the state obtained from $s$
by replacing $F_{i-1}$ copies of each of $F_{p-1}$ and $F_p$ by $F_{i-1}$ copies of $F_{p+1}$.
Then passing from $s$ to $t$ is a move, and $t$ has no copy of $F_{p-1}$, $F_{i-2}$ copies of
$F_p$ and $F_{i-1}$ copies of $F_{p+1}$.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Lemma 2.2.

articles.title: Two ones combine into a two in the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci
numbers as $F_1 = 1$, $F_2 = 2$, $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$. Passing from the state consisting of
two copies of $F_1$ to the state consisting of one copy of $F_2$ is a move of the Accelerated
Zeckendorf Game.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: Moves of the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci numbers as $F_1 = 1$,
$F_2 = 2$ and $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$, and call a finitely supported function
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a state, $s(i)$ being the number of copies of $F_i$. A move
takes a state $s$ to a state $t$ if for some multiplicity $m > 0$ one of the following holds:
the move $m \cdot C_i$ with $i \ge 2$, where $s(i-1) \ge m$, $s(i) \ge m$ and $t$ is
obtained from $s$ by removing $m$ copies each of $F_{i-1}$ and $F_i$ and adding $m$ copies
of $F_{i+1}$; the move $m \cdot C_1$, where $s(1) \ge 2m$ and $t$ is obtained by replacing
$2m$ copies of $F_1$ by $m$ copies of $F_2$; the move $m \cdot S_2$, where $s(2) \ge 2m$ and
$t$ is obtained by replacing $2m$ copies of $F_2$ by $m$ copies each of $F_1$ and $F_3$; or
the move $m \cdot S_i$ with $i \ge 3$, where $s(i) \ge 2m$ and $t$ is obtained by replacing
$2m$ copies of $F_i$ by $m$ copies each of $F_{i-2}$ and $F_{i+1}$.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: Unique losing move from $k$ copies of $F_2$ for odd $k$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be odd and $n \ge 2k$,
and suppose that for every $i < k$ with $3i \le n$ the state with $i$ copies of $F_3$,
$n - 3i$ copies of $F_1$ and nothing else is losing. Then $n \ge 3k$; the state $T$ with $k$
copies of $F_3$, $n - 3k$ copies of $F_1$ and nothing else is losing and is reached in one
move from the state $S$ with $k$ copies of $F_2$, $n - 2k$ copies of $F_1$ and nothing else;
and every losing state reached in one move from $S$ equals $T$.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Lemma 2.4.

articles.title: Unique winning first move
articles.statement:
For every $n$, if the state consisting of $n$ copies of $F_1$
is winning, then exactly one state reachable from it in one move is losing: when the first
player has a winning strategy in the game on $n$, exactly one first move preserves it.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Proposition 1.5.

articles.title: Characterization of winning states
articles.statement:
A state $s$ is winning if and only if some move
takes $s$ to a losing state.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 2.2, rules (3)-(4).

articles.title: The first player wins the game on $2$
articles.statement:
The state consisting of two copies of $F_1$ is
winning.

The winning move is $1 \cdot C_1$, which reaches the terminal state with one copy of $F_2$.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 2.2 (Player 1 wins for `n = 2`).

articles.title: Winning states of the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game
articles.statement:
A state $s$ is winning (the player
to move has a winning strategy) if some move takes $s$ to a losing state. Winning and losing
states are defined by simultaneous induction: a state is losing if every move from it reaches
a winning state.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 2.2 (rules (1)-(4) for winning and losing states).

articles.title: The complete game on $0$
articles.statement:
The sequence whose states are all the empty state is a
complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $0$ with $0$ moves.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: Complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Games
articles.statement:
A sequence of states $g_0, g_1, \dots$ is a
complete Accelerated Zeckendorf Game on $n$ with $L$ moves if $g_0$ consists of $n$ copies of
$F_1$, for every $j < L$ some move takes $g_j$ to $g_{j+1}$, and no move is possible from
$g_L$. The states after $g_L$ play no role.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: No move from the empty state
articles.statement:
No move takes the empty state (no copies of any $F_i$) to
any state.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: The Zeckendorf state of $4$
articles.statement:
The Zeckendorf state of $4$ consists of one copy of $F_3$
and one copy of $F_1$, reflecting the Zeckendorf decomposition $4 = F_3 + F_1 = 3 + 1$.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 1.1.

articles.title: The Zeckendorf state of zero is empty
articles.statement:
The Zeckendorf state of $0$ is the empty game
state, with no copies of any Fibonacci number.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Zeckendorf decomposition as a game state
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci numbers as $F_1 = 1$,
$F_2 = 2$ and $F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}$, and record a game state as a finitely supported
function $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, where $s(i)$ is the number of copies of $F_i$. Every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ has a unique Zeckendorf decomposition $n = F_{i_1} + \cdots + F_{i_r}$ with
$r \ge 0$, indices $i_1, \dots, i_r \ge 1$ and $i_t \ge i_{t+1} + 2$ for $1 \le t < r$. The
Zeckendorf state of $n$ is the game state with one copy of each $F_{i_t}$: $s(i) = 1$ if
$i \in \{i_1, \dots, i_r\}$ and $s(i) = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Diego Garcia-Fernandezsesma, Steven J. Miller, Thomas Rascon, Risa Vandegrift, and Ajmain Yamin, *The Accelerated Zeckendorf Game*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), no. 1, Article milleretal04072023, Section 1.1 and Theorem 1.3.

articles.title: Mex recursion for the Grundy number of a chocolate bar
articles.statement:
Let $f_1, \dots, f_s$ be
functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and write $G(x, z)$ for the Grundy number of the chocolate
bar with coordinates $x = (x_1, \dots, x_s) \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and width $z \in \mathbb{N}$. For
all $x$ and $z$, $G(x, z)$ is the least natural number $m$ such that $m \ne G(x', z)$ for every
$x'$ obtained from $x$ by replacing one coordinate $x_i$ with some $u < x_i$, and
$m \ne G(x^{(w)}, w)$ for every $w < z$, where $x^{(w)}_t = \min(x_t, f_t(w))$ for all $t$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definitions 9 and 10.

articles.title: The single bitter square has Grundy number zero
articles.statement:
For all functions
$f_1, \dots, f_s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the chocolate bar
$\mathrm{CB}(f_1, \dots, f_s, 0, \dots, 0, 0)$, whose coordinates and width are all $0$, has
Grundy number $0$: it is a single bitter square and has no move.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definitions 9 and 10.

articles.title: Grundy number of a chocolate bar
articles.statement:
Let $f_1, \dots, f_s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. For
coordinates $x = (x_1, \dots, x_s) \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and a width $z \in \mathbb{N}$, the position
$(x, z)$ stands for the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(f_1, \dots, f_s, x_1, \dots, x_s, z)$, whose
column at width $w \le z$ extends $\min(f_t(w), x_t) + 1$ cells along axis $t$. A move either
lowers one coordinate $x_i$ to some $u < x_i$, keeping the width $z$, or cuts the width to some
$w < z$, which replaces every $x_t$ by $\min(x_t, f_t(w))$. The Grundy number of $(x, z)$ is the
mex (least natural number not attained) of the Grundy numbers of the positions reachable from
$(x, z)$ in one move. It is defined for all $(x, z)$; the bars themselves are the positions with
$x_t \le f_t(z)$ for all $t$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definitions 2, 8, 9 and 10 (two functions) and Section 4, before Theorem 5 (four functions).

articles.title: Equal quotients by a power of two lie in one dyadic block
articles.statement:
Let $i$ be a natural number
and let $z < z'$ be natural numbers. Then $\lfloor z / 2^i \rfloor = \lfloor z' / 2^i \rfloor$ if
and only if there is a natural number $d$ with $d \cdot 2^i \le z$ and $z' < (d + 1) \cdot 2^i$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 8 (a).

articles.title: Mex step for chocolate bars with many functions
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number, let
$f_1, \dots, f_m : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ have the NS property, and let
$x_1, \dots, x_m, z, c$ be natural numbers with $x_t \le f_t(z)$ for all $t$ and
$c < x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_m \oplus z$, where $\oplus$ is nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or).
Then either there are an index $i$ and some $u < x_i$ such that $c$ is the nim-sum
$x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_m \oplus z$ with $x_i$ replaced by $u$, or there is some $w < z$
with $c = \min(x_1, f_1(w)) \oplus \cdots \oplus \min(x_m, f_m(w)) \oplus w$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Mex step for chocolate bars with two functions
articles.statement:
Let $g, h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
have the NS property, and let $x, y, z, c$ be natural numbers with $x \le g(z)$, $y \le h(z)$
and $c < x \oplus y \oplus z$, where $\oplus$ is nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or). Then
$c = u \oplus y \oplus z$ for some $u < x$, or $c = x \oplus v \oplus z$ for some $v < y$, or
$c = \min(g(w), x) \oplus \min(h(w), y) \oplus w$ for some $w < z$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 3 (b).

articles.title: Mex step for chocolate bars with one function
articles.statement:
Let $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ have
the NS property, and let $x, z, c$ be natural numbers with $x \le g(z)$ and $c < x \oplus z$,
where $\oplus$ is nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or). Then $c = u \oplus z$ for some $u < x$, or
$c = \min(g(w), x) \oplus w$ for some $w < z$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 3 (a).

articles.title: Dyadic splitting of two numbers with different quotients
articles.statement:
Let $z, z', i$ be natural
numbers with $\lfloor z / 2^i \rfloor < \lfloor z' / 2^i \rfloor$. Then there are natural numbers
$c$, $s$ and $t$ with $s \ge i$, $t < 2^s$, $z = c \cdot 2^{s+1} + t$ and
$c \cdot 2^{s+1} + 2^s \le z'$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 8 (b).

articles.title: Nim-sum Grundy numbers of chocolate bars with four functions
articles.statement:
Let
$f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4 : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone. Then all four have the NS property if
and only if, for all natural numbers $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4, z$ with $x_t \le f_t(z)$ for every $t$,
the Grundy number of the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4, x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4, z)$
equals $x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus x_4 \oplus z$, where $\oplus$ is nim-sum (bitwise
exclusive or).

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Nim-sum Grundy numbers of chocolate bars with two functions
articles.statement:
Let
$g, h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone. Then $g$ and $h$ both have the NS property if and
only if, for all natural numbers $x, y, z$ with $x \le g(z)$ and $y \le h(z)$, the Grundy number
of the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(g, h, x, y, z)$ equals $x \oplus y \oplus z$, where $\oplus$ is
nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or).

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Constant functions have the NS property
articles.statement:
For every natural number $c$, the constant
function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with value $c$ has the NS property.

## Sources

- characteristic lemma for the NS property of Miyadera, Manabe and Singh, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definition 11.

articles.title: Halving functions have the NS property
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m \ge 1$, the function
$x \mapsto \lfloor x / 2^m \rfloor$ on $\mathbb{N}$ has the NS property.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Constant extension preserves the NS property
articles.statement:
Let $z \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $h(a) \le h(b)$ whenever $a \le b \le z$, and
$\lfloor h(a) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor = \lfloor h(b) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor$ whenever $a, b \le z$,
$i \ge 1$ and $\lfloor a / 2^i \rfloor = \lfloor b / 2^i \rfloor$. Then the function sending
$x$ to $h(x)$ for $x \le z$ and to $h(z)$ for $x > z$ has the NS property.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 1.

articles.title: The NS property characterises nim-sum Grundy numbers of two-dimensional chocolate bars
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone. Then $f$ has the NS property if and only if, for
all $x, z \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \le f(z)$, the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(f, 0, x, 0, z)$ of
width $z$ (first function $f$, first coordinate $x$, second function constantly $0$, second
coordinate $0$) has Grundy number $x \oplus z$, where $\oplus$ denotes nim-sum (bitwise exclusive
or).

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Theorem 2.

articles.title: NS property
articles.statement:
A function $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has the *NS property* if it is
monotone (weakly increasing) and, for all $z, z' \in \mathbb{N}$ and every natural number
$i \ge 1$, $\lfloor z / 2^i \rfloor = \lfloor z' / 2^i \rfloor$ implies
$\lfloor h(z) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor = \lfloor h(z') / 2^{i-1} \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definition 11 (text of arXiv:2207.09134v1, NS property in Section 2).

articles.title: P-positions of a three-dimensional chocolate bar with floor-quotient height
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
natural number with $k \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and let $F(w, x) = \lfloor (w + x) / k \rfloor$. For
all $w, x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $y \le F(w, x)$, the three-dimensional chocolate bar
$\mathrm{CB}(F, w, x, y)$ has Grundy number $0$ (is a P-position) if and only if
$w \oplus x \oplus y = 0$, where $\oplus$ denotes nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or).

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Mex recursion for chocolate bars with a height function
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$, and write $G(x, y)$ for the Grundy number of the chocolate bar
$\mathrm{CB}(F, x_1, \dots, x_s, y)$. For all $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $y \in \mathbb{N}$,
$G(x, y)$ is the least natural number $m$ such that $m \ne G(x', \min(F(x'), y))$ for every $x'$
obtained from $x$ by lowering one coordinate $x_i$ to some $u < x_i$, and $m \ne G(x, v)$ for
every $v < y$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definition 17.

articles.title: The single bitter cube has Grundy number zero
articles.statement:
For every $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and every
$F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$, the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(F, 0, \dots, 0, 0)$ has no move,
so its Grundy number is $0$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definition 17.

articles.title: Grundy number of a chocolate bar with a height function
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$. The $(s + 1)$-dimensional chocolate bar
$\mathrm{CB}(F, x_1, \dots, x_s, y)$ has, at each $u = (u_1, \dots, u_s)$ with $u_t \le x_t$ for
all $t$, a column of height $\min(F(u), y) + 1$. A move either lowers one coordinate $x_i$ to some
$a < x_i$, which clamps the height to $\min(F(x'), y)$ for the new position $x'$, or lowers the
height $y$ to some $v < y$. The Grundy number of $\mathrm{CB}(F, x_1, \dots, x_s, y)$ is the mex
(least natural number not attained) of the Grundy numbers of the positions reachable in one
move. It is defined for all $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $y \in \mathbb{N}$; the bars themselves are
the positions with $y \le F(x)$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definitions 15, 16 and 17 (and Definition 13 with second function `0`).

articles.title: Nim-sum sets under clamping by functions with the NS property
articles.statement:
Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1} : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ have the NS property, and let
$x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}, z \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $x_t \le f_t(z)$ for every $t < m$. Then

$$
\{x_0 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_{m-1} \oplus w : w < z\} =
\{\min(x_0, f_0(w)) \oplus \cdots \oplus \min(x_{m-1}, f_{m-1}(w)) \oplus w : w < z\},
$$

where $\oplus$ denotes nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or).

The printed left-hand nim-sum carries a stray index $j \ne i$ with $i$ unbound; it is read as the
full nim-sum, as in Lemma 5 (the case of two functions), which the proof generalises.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Nim-sum image identity for one NS function
articles.statement:
Let $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ have the
NS property and let $x, z \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \le g(z)$. Writing $\oplus$ for the nim-sum
(bitwise exclusive or) of natural numbers, the sets $\{x \oplus w : w < z\}$ and
$\{\min(g(w), x) \oplus w : w < z\}$ are equal, where $w$ ranges over the natural numbers.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 5, equation (20).

articles.title: Nim-sum image identity for two NS functions
articles.statement:
Let $g, h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ have
the NS property and let $x, y, z \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \le g(z)$ and $y \le h(z)$. Writing
$\oplus$ for the nim-sum (bitwise exclusive or) of natural numbers, the sets
$\{x \oplus y \oplus w : w < z\}$ and $\{\min(g(w), x) \oplus \min(h(w), y) \oplus w : w < z\}$
are equal, where $w$ ranges over the natural numbers.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 5, equation (19).

articles.title: Indicator functions with the NS property
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone,
with $f(x) \le 1$ for all $x$ and $f(x) = 1$ for some $x$. Then $f$ has the NS property if and
only if there is an even $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $f$ is the indicator function of
$\{n \in \mathbb{N} : n \ge m\}$, that is, $f(n) = 1$ for $n \ge m$ and $f(n) = 0$ for $n < m$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 9.

articles.title: Height-one chocolate bars with nim-sum Grundy numbers
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone for the coordinatewise order, with $F(x) \le 1$ for
all $x$. For $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$, $i < s$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$ write $x[i \mapsto t]$ for $x$
with its $i$-th coordinate replaced by $t$, and suppose that for all $x$ and $i$ there is a $t$
with $F(x[i \mapsto t]) = 1$. Write $\oplus$ for nim-sum. Then the following are equivalent:
(a) for all $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $i < s$ there is an even $m \in \mathbb{N}$ (depending on $x$
and $i$) such that $F(x[i \mapsto t]) = 1$ for $t \ge m$ and $F(x[i \mapsto t]) = 0$ for $t < m$;
(b) for all $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $y \le F(x)$, the Grundy number of the
chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(F, x_0, \dots, x_{s-1}, y)$ is
$x_0 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_{s-1} \oplus y$.

The hypothesis that every section takes the value $1$ is that of Lemma 9, from which the
corollary is derived.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Taking a minimum preserves quotients by powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c, k \in \mathbb{N}$. If
$\lfloor a / 2^k \rfloor = \lfloor b / 2^k \rfloor$, then
$\lfloor \min(a, c) / 2^k \rfloor = \lfloor \min(b, c) / 2^k \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 2 (i).

articles.title: Quotients of a truncated NS function by powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
have the NS property and let $z, z', k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \ge 1$ and
$\lfloor z' / 2^k \rfloor = \lfloor z / 2^k \rfloor$. Then for every $y \in \mathbb{N}$,
$\lfloor \min(h(z'), y) / 2^{k-1} \rfloor = \lfloor \min(h(z), y) / 2^{k-1} \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 2 (ii).

articles.title: Nim with a restricted pass
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}^s$ with $m_i > 0$
for every $i < s$, and let $F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$ be the pass indicator of $m$:
$F(x) = 1$ if $m_j \le x_j$ for some $j$, and $F(x) = 0$ otherwise. Write $\oplus$ for nim-sum.
Then the following are equivalent: (a) for all $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $p \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$p \le F(x)$, the Grundy number of the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(F, x_0, \dots, x_{s-1}, p)$ is
$x_0 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_{s-1} \oplus p$; (b) $m_i$ is even for every $i < s$.

The bar is Nim on $s$ piles with a one-time pass usable only while $F(x) = 1$: removing stones
from a pile, reaching $x'$, replaces $p$ by $\min(F(x'), p)$, and the pass lowers $p$ from $1$
to $0$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Corollary 2.

articles.title: The Nim pass indicator is at most one
articles.statement:
For every $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and all
$m, x \in \mathbb{N}^s$, the pass indicator of $m$ at $x$ is at most $1$; that is, it takes values
in $\{0, 1\}$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 10 (the function `F`).

articles.title: Sections of the Nim pass indicator with the NS property
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$m \in \mathbb{N}^s$ with $m_i > 0$ for every $i < s$, and let $F : \mathbb{N}^s \to \mathbb{N}$ be
the pass indicator of $m$: $F(x) = 1$ if $m_j \le x_j$ for some $j$, and $F(x) = 0$ otherwise.
For $x \in \mathbb{N}^s$, $i < s$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$ write $x[i \mapsto t]$ for $x$ with its
$i$-th coordinate replaced by $t$. Then the following are equivalent: (a) for all
$x \in \mathbb{N}^s$ and $i < s$, the function $t \mapsto F(x[i \mapsto t])$ has the NS property;
(b) $m_i$ is even for every $i < s$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 10.

articles.title: The pass is unavailable from the empty position
articles.statement:
Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$m \in \mathbb{N}^s$ with $m_i > 0$ for every $i < s$. Then the pass indicator of $m$ takes the
value $0$ at the zero tuple $(0, \dots, 0)$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 10 (the function `F`).

articles.title: Pass indicator of Nim with a restricted pass
articles.statement:
For $s$ piles with thresholds
$m_0, \dots, m_{s-1}$ and pile sizes $x_0, \dots, x_{s-1}$ (natural numbers), the pass
indicator is $1$ if $m_j \le x_j$ for some pile $j$ (the pass may be used), and $0$ if
$x_j < m_j$ for every pile $j$.

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Lemma 10 and Corollary 2 (the function `F`).

articles.title: The identity function lacks the NS property
articles.statement:
The identity function on the natural
numbers does not have the NS property: $\lfloor 0/2 \rfloor = \lfloor 1/2 \rfloor$, but
$0 \ne 1$.

## Sources

- characteristic lemma for the NS property of Miyadera, Manabe and Singh, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Definition 11.

articles.title: NS property of sections and the three-dimensional chocolate bar
articles.statement:
Let
$F : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotone for the componentwise order. Then
the sections $x \mapsto F(n, x)$ and $w \mapsto F(w, n)$ have the NS property for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ if and only if, for all natural numbers $w$, $x$, $y$ with $y \le F(w, x)$,
the Grundy number of the chocolate bar $\mathrm{CB}(F, w, x, y)$, whose column at $(u, v)$
(with $u \le w$, $v \le x$) has height $\min(F(u, v), y) + 1$, equals the nim-sum
$w \oplus x \oplus y$ (bitwise exclusive or).

## Sources

- Ryohei Miyadera, Hikaru Manabe and Aditi Singh, *Generalizations of Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Chocolate Bar Games*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article G3, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Every finite set contains a copy of the empty set
articles.statement:
Every finite set $M$ of natural
numbers contains a homothetic copy of the empty set.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 1.

articles.title: Containing a homothetic copy
articles.statement:
Let $S$ and $M$ be finite sets of natural numbers. $M$
contains a homothetic copy of $S$ if there are a natural number $a > 0$ and an integer $b$ such
that $as + b \in M$ for every $s \in S$, that is, $aS + b \subseteq M$. This is Maker's winning
condition.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 1.

articles.title: Every finite set of rationals is a copy of itself
articles.statement:
For every finite set $A$ of rational
numbers, $A$ is a copy of $A$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 5.

articles.title: Copies of finite sets of rationals
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of rational numbers.
$B$ is a copy of $A$ if there are rationals $a > 0$ and $b$ such that
$B = aA + b = \{ax + b : x \in A\}$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 5.

articles.title: Reflections of finite sets of rationals
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of rational
numbers. $B$ is a reflection of $A$ if there are rationals $a < 0$ and $b$ such that
$B = aA + b = \{ax + b : x \in A\}$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 6.

articles.title: A fast Maker win forces symmetry
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers with at
least two elements. If Maker, moving first with no numbers claimed, can force a win in the
game on $S$ within $|S|$ selections, then $S$, viewed as a set of rational numbers, is
symmetric.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Possible types of a symmetric set
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of rational numbers with
$n \ge 4$ elements. If $S$ is symmetric of type $(i, j)$, with positions counted from $0$, then
$(i, j)$ is $(0, n - 1)$, $(1, n - 1)$ or $(0, n - 2)$. In the paper's one-based numbering these
are the types $(1, n)$, $(2, n)$ and $(1, n - 1)$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the symmetry type
articles.statement:
A finite set $S$ of rational numbers with at least
four elements is symmetric of at most one type: if $S$ is symmetric of types $(i, j)$ and
$(i', j')$, then $i = i'$ and $j = j'$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Symmetric sets of a given type
articles.statement:
Let $S = \{s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_{n-1}\}$ be a finite
set of $n$ rational numbers and let $i, j < n$. Then $S$ is called symmetric of type $(i, j)$ if
$i < j$ and $S \setminus \{s_i\}$ is a copy of $S \setminus \{s_j\}$.

Positions are counted from $0$, so the paper's type $(i + 1, j + 1)$ is the type $(i, j)$ here.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Definition 2.

articles.title: Symmetric sets of rationals
articles.statement:
A finite set $S$ of rational numbers is symmetric if it is
symmetric of some type $(i, j)$ with $i, j < |S|$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Definition 2.

articles.title: Maker wins the $S$-game in $|S|$ moves when $|S| \le 3$
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a finite set of
natural numbers with $|S| \le 3$, then, starting from the position where no number has been
claimed, Maker wins the $S$-game within $|S|$ moves.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Maker wins the $S$-game in five moves when $|S| = 4$
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a set of four natural
numbers, then, starting from the position where no number has been claimed, Maker wins the
$S$-game within $5$ moves.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Four-element sets with a four-move win are the symmetric ones
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a set of four
natural numbers, then, starting from the position where no number has been claimed, Maker wins
the $S$-game within $4$ moves if and only if $S$, viewed as a set of rationals, is symmetric.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Hales–Jewett bound for the $S$-game
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers with
$|S| = n$, and let $N$ be a natural number such that every 2-coloring of $S^N$ has a
monochromatic combinatorial line. Then, starting from the position where no number has been
claimed, Maker wins the $S$-game within $\lceil n^N / 2 \rceil$ moves.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Tree criterion for fast wins
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers and $p$ a
natural number. Let $T$ be a finite rooted tree with root $r$ whose vertices are pairwise
distinct rationals, such that every path from $r$ down to a vertex has at most $p$ vertices and
some such path has exactly $p$ vertices (so $T$ has height $p - 1$). Suppose that for every leaf
$v$ the set of vertices on the path from $r$ to $v$ contains a copy $aS + b$ of $S$ with
rationals $a > 0$ and $b$, and that every vertex other than the root that is not a leaf has at
least two children. Then, starting from the position where no number has been claimed, Maker
wins the $S$-game within $p$ moves.

The tree is given by the finite set of its root-to-vertex paths, each recorded as the list of
rationals along it.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Winning within zero moves
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers, and let $M$ and
$B$ be finite sets of natural numbers. Maker wins the $S$-game within $0$ moves from the position
where Maker has claimed $M$ and Breaker has claimed $B$ if and only if $M$ contains a copy
$aS + b = \{as + b : s \in S\}$ of $S$, where $a$ is a positive integer and $b$ is an integer.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Section 5.

articles.title: Maker wins within $p$ moves
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers. In the
$S$-game, Maker and Breaker alternately claim unclaimed natural numbers, and Maker wins once the
numbers Maker has claimed contain a copy $aS + b = \{as + b : s \in S\}$ of $S$, where $a$ is a
positive integer and $b$ is an integer. Let $M$ and $B$ be finite sets of natural numbers
(claimed by Maker and by Breaker) and $p$ a natural number, with Maker to move. Maker wins
within $p$ moves if $M$ already contains such a copy of $S$, or if $p \ge 1$ and there is a
number $x \notin M \cup B$ such that for every number $y \ne x$ with $y \notin M \cup B$, Maker
wins within $p - 1$ moves from the position where Maker has claimed $M \cup \{x\}$ and Breaker
has claimed $B \cup \{y\}$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Sections 1 and 5 (`p`-move strategy).

articles.title: Maker cannot win the $S$-game in $|S|$ moves when $|S| \ge 5$
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a finite
set of natural numbers with $|S| \ge 5$, then, starting from the position where no number has
been claimed, Maker does not win the $S$-game within $|S|$ moves.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Theorem 5.

articles.title: The zero-geometric set $S_2(n + 2, k)$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every rational
$k$, $S_2(n + 2, k) = \{0\} \cup \{k^i : 0 \le i \le n\} = \{0, 1, k, \dots, k^n\}$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Definition 3.

articles.title: Zero-geometric copies of symmetric sets
articles.statement:
Let $S = \{s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_{n-1}\}$ be a
finite set of $n$ rational numbers, and let $i, j < n$ be such that $S$ is symmetric of type
$(i, j)$, with positions counted from $0$. If $i = 1$ and $j = n - 1$, then there is a rational
number $k > 1$ such that the zero-geometric set $S_2(n, k)$ is a copy of $S$. If $i = 0$ and
$j = n - 2$, then there is a rational number $k > 1$ such that $S_2(n, k)$ is a reflection of $S$.

In the paper's one-based numbering these are the types $(2, n)$ and $(1, n - 1)$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Lemma 4.

articles.title: The zero-geometric set $S_2(1, k)$ is $\{0\}$
articles.statement:
For every rational number $k$, the
zero-geometric set $S_2(1, k)$ equals $\{0\}$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Definition 3.

articles.title: The zero-geometric set $S_2(n, k)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a rational number $k$,
$S_2(n, k)$ is the finite set of rationals $\{0\} \cup \{k^i : 0 \le i < n - 1\}$, that is,
$\{0, 1, k, \dots, k^{n-2}\}$ when $n \ge 2$ and $\{0\}$ when $n \le 1$.

## Sources

- Alpert, Barham, Freidin, Tan, and Weiner, *Fast Winning Strategies in a Generalized van der Waerden Game*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A40, Definition 3.

articles.title: Levels of the branches of an arch
articles.statement:
On numerator–denominator pairs write
$s(x, y) = (x, x + y)$ for the son and $t(x, y) = (x + y, y)$ for the daughter of a vertex of the
Calkin–Wilf tree. Let $a, b, c, d, k$ be natural numbers with $0 < b < a$ and $0 < c < d$. Then
$t(s^k(a - b, b))$, the daughter of the $k$-fold son of $(a - b, b)$, has first entry
$(k+1)a - kb$ and second entry $ka - (k-1)b$, and $s(t^k(c, d - c))$, the son of the $k$-fold
daughter of $(c, d - c)$, has first entry $kd - (k-1)c$ and second entry $(k+1)d - kc$, the
right-hand sides computed in the integers.

When $a/b$ and $c/d$ are the left and right tops of an arch, these pairs are level $k$ (level $0$
the top) of its left branch, which descends by nieces, and of its right branch, which descends by
nephews; the formulas hold without the arch-top hypothesis.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Lemma 5.1.

articles.title: The first rows of the Calkin–Wilf tree
articles.statement:
As lists of numerator–denominator pairs, row $1$
of the Calkin–Wilf tree is $(1, 2), (2, 1)$ and row $2$ is $(1, 3), (3, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)$, in
this order.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 2.

articles.title: Rows of the Calkin–Wilf tree
articles.statement:
Row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree is a list of
numerator–denominator pairs, the pair $(a, b)$ standing for $a/b$. Row $0$ is the single pair
$(1, 1)$, and row $k + 1$ is obtained from row $k$ by replacing each pair $(a, b)$, in order, by
its two children $(a, a + b)$ and $(a + b, b)$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 2.

articles.title: Continued fractions with maximal optimal play in Euclid
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$a_0, \dots, a_r$ write $[a_0, \dots, a_r]$ for the continued fraction
$a_0 + 1/(a_1 + 1/(\cdots + 1/a_r))$, and $1^j$ for a block of $j$ ones; read a positive rational
$u/v$ in lowest terms as the position $(u, v)$ of the Euclid game. Let $n \ge 1$, $i$ and $k$ be
natural numbers. If the position of $[1^{n-1}, 2]$ lies in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree, its
Smith remoteness is $k$. If the position of $[1^{n-1}, 3]$ lies in row $k$, its Smith remoteness
is less than $k$. If $1 \le i \le n - 2$ and the position of $[1^i, 2, 1^{n-2-i}, 2]$ lies in
row $k$, its Smith remoteness is $k$ when $i \equiv n \pmod 2$ and less than $k$ when
$i \not\equiv n \pmod 2$.

Proposition 6.6 also identifies these pairs as the ones taking the most steps in the Euclidean
algorithm, a result of Hopkins and Tangboonduangjit; that half is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 6.6.

articles.title: Number of arch tops in a row of the Calkin–Wilf tree
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 2$ let $T_k$ be the
number of vertices of row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree of the form $(2m+n)/(m+n)$ with $m/n$ a
P-position of Euclid in row $k - 2$. Then $3T_k = 2^{k-2} + 2(-1)^k$, that is,
$T_k = 2^{k-2}/3 + 2(-1)^k/3$.

The vertex $(2m+n)/(m+n)$ is the son's daughter of $m/n$, the left top of the arch below $m/n$;
the daughter's son $(m+n)/(m+2n)$ is the right top, so $T_k$ counts the arches whose tops lie in
row $k$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Corollary 4.7.

articles.title: Number of P-positions of Euclid in a row of the Calkin–Wilf tree
articles.statement:
Let $L_k$ be the
number of P-positions of Euclid in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree. Then $L_0 = 1$, $L_1 = 0$,
$L_{k+2} = L_{k+1} + 2L_k$ for every $k$, and $3L_k = 2^k + 2(-1)^k$ for every $k$, that is,
$L_k = 2^k/3 + 2(-1)^k/3$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Corollary 4.6.

articles.title: Positions of a Calkin–Wilf row with maximal optimal play in Euclid
articles.statement:
For every $k \ge 0$,
the number of positions in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree whose Smith remoteness in the Euclid
game is $k$ equals $2^{k/2}$ if $k$ is even and $2^{(k+1)/2}$ if $k$ is odd.

Smith remoteness is the length of optimal play when the winner hurries and the loser delays.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 6.1.

articles.title: The game Euclid
articles.statement:
Euclid as an impartial game: its positions are the pairs $(a, b)$ of
natural numbers, its moves from $(a, b)$ are the Euclid moves, the rank of $(a, b)$ is $a + b$,
and its starting position is $(1, 1)$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Euclid moves lower the sum
articles.statement:
If $(a', b')$ is a Euclid move from $(a, b)$, then
$a' + b' < a + b$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Euclid moves
articles.statement:
The moves of Euclid from a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers are as follows.
If $a = b$, $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, there are none. If $0 < a < b$, the moves are to the pairs
$(a, b - ja)$ for every integer $j \ge 1$ with $ja < b$; if $0 < b < a$, the moves are to the
pairs $(a - jb, b)$ for every integer $j \ge 1$ with $jb < a$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Aunt or cousin of a P-position
articles.statement:
Call a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers a P-position when
the Euclid P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$, and let its son be $s(a, b) = (a, a + b)$ and
its daughter $d(a, b) = (a + b, b)$, as in the Calkin–Wilf tree. Let $x, y$ be positive integers,
let $r = (x, y)$, let $q$ be one of the two children $s(r)$ and $d(r)$ of $r$, and let $q'$ be the
other one. If the daughter $d(q)$ is a P-position, then exactly one of its aunt $q'$ and its male
cousin $s(q')$ is a P-position. If the son $s(q)$ is a P-position, then exactly one of its uncle
$q'$ and its female cousin $d(q')$ is a P-position.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 4.3.

articles.title: Correctness of the fuel-bounded Euclid classifier
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $f$, $a$ and $b$
with $a + b \le f$, the fuel-bounded evaluation of the P-positions of Euclid with fuel $f$ returns
true at $(a, b)$ if and only if $(a, b)$ is a normal-play P-position of the Euclid game.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Euclid classifier
articles.statement:
The fuel-bounded evaluation of the P-positions of Euclid is
the function $E(f, a, b)$ of natural numbers $f, a, b$ with Boolean values defined by recursion on
the fuel $f$. With no fuel, $E(0, a, b)$ is true. Otherwise $E(f + 1, a, b)$ is true when $a = b$,
$a = 0$ or $b = 0$; when $0 < a < b$ it is true iff $E(f, a, b - ja)$ is false for every $j \ge 1$
with $ja < b$; and when $0 < b < a$ it is true iff $E(f, a - jb, b)$ is false for every $j \ge 1$
with $jb < a$.

In Euclid a move replaces the larger entry by its difference with a positive multiple of the
smaller one, keeping both entries positive, and the player facing two equal entries (no move)
loses. With fuel at least $a + b$ the value is exact.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Establishing branches: nieces and nephews of P-positions
articles.statement:
Call a pair $(a, b)$ of natural
numbers a P-position when the Euclid P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$, and read it as the
vertex $a/b$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree, with son $a/(a+b)$ and daughter $(a+b)/b$. Let $x, y$ be
positive integers. If the daughter $(x+y)/y$ of $x/y$ is a P-position, then so is its niece
$(2x+y)/(x+y)$, the daughter of its sibling $x/(x+y)$. If the son $x/(x+y)$ of $x/y$ is a
P-position, then so is its nephew $(x+y)/(x+2y)$, the son of its sibling $(x+y)/y$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 4.2.

articles.title: The Euclid P-position test is correct
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the Euclid
P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$ if and only if $(a, b)$ is a normal-play P-position of
the Euclid game.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Self-similarity of the P-positions of Euclid
articles.statement:
Call a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers a
P-position when the Euclid P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$, and read it as the vertex
$a/b$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree, with son $a/(a+b)$ and daughter $(a+b)/b$. Let $V$ be a vertex in
some row of the Calkin–Wilf tree that is a P-position. Then for every finite sequence $w$ of steps,
each step going to the son or to the daughter, the vertex reached from $V$ by following $w$ is a
P-position if and only if the vertex reached from the root $1/1$ by following $w$ is one.

In other words, below every P-position the P-positions sit exactly where they sit below the root.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Theorem 4.5.

articles.title: Small P-positions of Euclid
articles.statement:
The Euclid P-position test returns true at the pairs $(1, 1)$
and $(3, 2)$ and false at the pairs $(2, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Distinguishing the tops of arches
articles.statement:
Call a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers a P-position
when the Euclid P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$, and read it as the vertex $a/b$ of the
Calkin–Wilf tree, with son $a/(a+b)$ and daughter $(a+b)/b$. Let $m, n$ be positive integers. If
$m/n$ is a P-position, then so are its son's daughter $(2m+n)/(m+n)$ and its daughter's son
$(m+n)/(m+2n)$.

The statement covers all positive pairs; the tree vertices are the coprime ones.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 4.1.

articles.title: Euclid P-position test
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the Euclid P-position test at
$(a, b)$ is the value at $(a, b)$ of the fuel-bounded evaluation of the P-positions of Euclid with
fuel $a + b$.

It is true exactly at the P-positions of Euclid, the positions from which every move leads to a
position that is not a P-position: each move lowers $a + b$, so fuel $a + b$ suffices.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: The Fibonacci arches
articles.statement:
Let $F_j$ be the Fibonacci numbers with $F_0 = F_1 = 1$ and
$F_{j+2} = F_{j+1} + F_j$. Call a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers a P-position when the Euclid
P-position test returns true at $(a, b)$, read it as the vertex $a/b$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree, and
let $s(a/b) = a/(a+b)$ be its son and $d(a/b) = (a+b)/b$ its daughter; write $s^k$ and $d^k$ for
the $k$-fold iterates. Let $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 0$, and let $V = F_{2n-1}/F_{2n-2}$. Then $V$ is a
P-position, its son's daughter $d(s(V))$ is $F_{2n+1}/F_{2n}$, and its daughter's son $s(d(V))$
is $F_{2n}/(F_{2n} + F_{2n-2})$. The vertex $L = d(s^k((F_{2n+1} - F_{2n})/F_{2n}))$ is a
P-position whose numerator is $F_{2n+1} + kF_{2n-1}$ and whose denominator is
$F_{2n+1} + (k-1)F_{2n-1}$, and the vertex $R = s(d^k(F_{2n}/F_{2n-2}))$ is the P-position
$(F_{2n} + kF_{2n-2})/(F_{2n} + (k+1)F_{2n-2})$.

Here $L$ and $R$ are level $k$ (level $0$ the top) of the left and right branches of the arch
topped by $d(s(V))$ and $s(d(V))$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 5.2.

articles.title: Fibonacci arch tops
articles.statement:
Index the Fibonacci numbers as in the source, $F_0 = F_1 = 1$ and
$F_{j+2} = F_{j+1} + F_j$. Write $a/b$ for the position $(a, b)$ of Euclid, and call $a/(a+b)$
its son and $(a+b)/b$ its daughter. Let $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 0$ be integers, and let
$X = (F_{2n+1} + kF_{2n-1})/(F_{2n+1} + (k-1)F_{2n-1})$ and
$Y = (F_{2n} + kF_{2n-2})/(F_{2n} + (k+1)F_{2n-2})$. Then $X$ is a P-position of Euclid, and so
are its son's daughter $(3F_{2n+1} + (3k-1)F_{2n-1})/(2F_{2n+1} + (2k-1)F_{2n-1})$ and its
daughter's son $(2F_{2n+1} + (2k-1)F_{2n-1})/(3F_{2n+1} + (3k-2)F_{2n-1})$. Likewise $Y$ is a
P-position of Euclid, and so are its son's daughter
$(3F_{2n} + (3k+1)F_{2n-2})/(2F_{2n} + (2k+1)F_{2n-2})$ and its daughter's son
$(2F_{2n} + (2k+1)F_{2n-2})/(3F_{2n} + (3k+2)F_{2n-2})$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Corollary 5.3.

articles.title: Golden-ratio bounds for N-positions of maximal remoteness below 1
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. If the pair $(m, n)$, read as the fraction $m/n$, lies in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf
tree, $m < n$, the position $(m, n)$ of Euclid is not a P-position, and its Smith remoteness in
Euclid equals $k$, then $1/(\varphi + 1) < m/n < 1/\varphi$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Corollary 6.4.

articles.title: Golden-ratio bounds for N-positions of maximal remoteness above 1
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. If the pair $(m, n)$, read as the fraction $m/n$, lies in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf
tree, $n < m$, the position $(m, n)$ of Euclid is not a P-position, and its Smith remoteness in
Euclid equals $k$, then $\varphi < m/n < \varphi + 1$.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 6.3.

articles.title: Golden-ratio bounds for P-positions of maximal remoteness
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden
ratio. If the pair $(m, n)$, read as the fraction $m/n$, lies in row $k$ of the Calkin–Wilf tree,
$m \ne n$, the position $(m, n)$ of Euclid is a P-position, and its Smith remoteness in Euclid
equals $k$, then $(\varphi + 2)/(\varphi + 1) < m/n < \varphi$ or
$1/\varphi < m/n < (\varphi + 1)/(\varphi + 2)$.

The hypothesis $m \ne n$ corrects the printed statement, which fails at the root $1/1$ (a
P-position with $0$ moves in row $0$, and $1$ lies in neither interval).

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 6.5.

articles.title: Maximal-remoteness paths alternate in pairs
articles.statement:
In the Calkin–Wilf tree the vertex $a/b$ has
son $a/(a+b)$ and daughter $(a+b)/b$. Let $w = (w_0, \dots, w_{\ell-1})$ be a sequence of steps,
each "son" or "daughter", and let $a/b$ be the vertex reached from the root $1/1$ by following
$w$. If the Smith remoteness of the position $(a, b)$ of Euclid equals $\ell$, then
$w_{2i} \ne w_{2i+1}$ for every $i$ with $2i + 1 < \ell$; that is, steps $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ are
one son step and one daughter step, in either order.

## Sources

- Michael A. Jones and Brittany C. Ohlinger, *Self-Similar Structure of P-Positions of the Game Euclid*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62.1 (2024), Proposition 6.2.

articles.title: Edges of the complete graph $K_n$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the complete board is the
finite set of edges of the complete graph $K_n$ on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, that is,
the set of all unordered pairs $\{i, j\}$ of distinct vertices $i \ne j$.

articles.title: Free elements of a position
articles.statement:
For finite sets $X$ (the board), $M$ (the elements claimed
by Maker) and $R$ (the elements claimed by Breaker), the free elements are the elements of $X$
claimed by neither player, that is, the set $X \setminus (M \cup R)$.

articles.title: Maker's Hamiltonicity target
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a set $C$ of unordered pairs of
vertices from $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ meets the Hamiltonicity target when the simple graph on
these $n$ vertices whose edges are the pairs of distinct vertices in $C$ is Hamiltonian: it has a
cycle passing through every vertex exactly once, with the convention that the one-vertex graph is
Hamiltonian.

articles.title: The critical bias of the Hamiltonicity game is $(1 + o(1))\, n / \ln n$
articles.statement:
Consider the
$(1 : b)$ Maker-Breaker game on the edges of the complete graph $K_n$ in which Breaker moves
first: Breaker claims $b$ free edges per turn (all remaining free edges if fewer than $b$ are
left), Maker claims one free edge per turn, and Maker wins if, once every edge is claimed, his
edges contain a Hamilton cycle. For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $n_0$ such that for
every $n \ge n_0$, Maker has a winning strategy for every natural number $b$ with
$0 < b \le (1 - \varepsilon)\, n / \ln n$, and Maker has no winning strategy for any natural
number $b \ge (1 + \varepsilon)\, n / \ln n$.

Maker's side is Krivelevich's Theorem 1, which gives Maker a win for every
$b \le (1 - 30 / \ln^{1/4} n)\, n / \ln n$ once $n$ is large. Breaker's side follows from the
Chvátal-Erdős Theorem 3.1, whose Breaker strategy claims every edge at some vertex for every
$b > (1 + \varepsilon / 2)\, n / \ln n$ once $n$ is large.

## Sources

- T. Szabó (joint with H. Gebauer and M. Krivelevich), Thresholds for positional games, in Combinatorics, Oberwolfach Reports 5 (2008), no. 1, pp. 56-59, DOI 10.4171/OWR/2008/01; resolution: M. Krivelevich, The critical bias for the Hamiltonicity game is (1 + o(1)) n / ln n, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 24 (2011), 125-131, DOI 10.1090/S0894-0347-2010-00678-9, arXiv:0909.2744; V. Chvátal and P. Erdős, Biased positional games, Ann. Discrete Math. 2 (1978), 221-229, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-06.pdf, Krivelevich, Section 1 (Breaker moves first) and Theorem 1 (Maker wins for b ≤ (1 - 30/ln^{1/4} n) n/ln n); Chvátal-Erdős, Section 1 (Breaker moves first) and Theorem 3.1 (Breaker wins T(n, b) for b > (1 + ε) n/log n and n > n₀(ε), by isolating a vertex); report p. 57 (the Hamiltonicity game is harder for Maker than the connectivity game), https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.2744.

articles.title: The Hamiltonicity critical-bias property
articles.statement:
This is the statement that the critical bias of
the Hamiltonicity game is $(1 + o(1))\, n / \ln n$. In the $(1 : b)$ Maker-Breaker game on the
edges of the complete graph $K_n$ with Breaker moving first, Breaker claims $b$ free edges per
turn (all remaining free edges if fewer than $b$ are left), Maker claims one free edge per turn,
and Maker wins if, once every edge is claimed, his edges contain a Hamilton cycle. The property
says that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $n_0$ such that for every $n \ge n_0$, Maker
has a winning strategy for every natural number $b$ with $0 < b \le (1 - \varepsilon)\, n / \ln n$,
and Maker has no winning strategy for any natural number $b \ge (1 + \varepsilon)\, n / \ln n$.

articles.title: Maker can force a win in the biased Maker-Breaker game
articles.statement:
Fix a finite board $X$, a bias
$b \in \mathbb{N}$ and a property of finite sets, Maker's target. At a position $(M, R)$, where
$M$ and $R$ are the sets claimed so far by Maker and by Breaker, an element of $X$ is free if it
lies in neither $M$ nor $R$. The relation "Maker, to move at $(M, R)$, can force a win" is the
least one satisfying two rules: it holds when no element of $X$ is free and $M$ satisfies the
target; and it holds when there is a free element $e$ such that, for every set $R'$ of exactly
$\min(b, r)$ of the $r$ elements that are free after $e$ is claimed, Maker can force a win at
$(M \cup \{e\}, R \cup R')$. Thus Maker claims one free element per turn, Breaker answers with
$b$ of them (all remaining ones if fewer are free), play ends when the board is exhausted, and
Maker wins if his set satisfies the target.

articles.title: Maker wins the biased game with Breaker moving first
articles.statement:
For a finite board $X$, a bias
$b \in \mathbb{N}$ and a target property of Maker's claimed set, Maker wins the $(1 : b)$
Maker-Breaker game on $X$ in which Breaker moves first when, for every set $F \subseteq X$ of
exactly $\min(b, |X|)$ elements that Breaker may claim in his first move, Maker can force a win
when it is his turn at the position where he has claimed nothing and Breaker has claimed $F$.

Breaker moving first is the convention of both sources (Krivelevich, Section 1: "We assume that
Breaker moves first"; Chvátal-Erdős, Section 1: "with the Breaker going first").

articles.title: The set $Y_{aabc}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $Y_{aabc}$ when there is an index $i$ with $a_{i+2} \equiv a_i + 2 \pmod 4$
and $a_{i+1} \equiv a_{i-1} + 1 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `Y_{aabc}`).

articles.title: The complement set $(\hat Y_{abab})^c$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position
$a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$
of $C_4$ lies in $(\hat Y_{abab})^c$ when its total $a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3$ is even and $a$ does
not lie in $\hat Y_{abab}$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `(\hat Y_{abab})^c`).

articles.title: The set $\hat Y_{abab}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$ lies in
$\hat Y_{abab}$ when $a_0 \equiv a_2 \pmod 4$ and $a_1 \equiv a_3 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `\hat Y_{abab}`).

articles.title: The set $\hat Y_{abac}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $\hat Y_{abac}$ when there is an index $i$ with $a_i \equiv a_{i+2} \pmod 4$
and $a_{i+1} \equiv a_{i-1} + 1 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `\hat Y_{abac}`).

articles.title: Examples of positions in the sets $Y$ for $C_4$
articles.statement:
Writing $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ for the
position with $a_j$ pebbles on vertex $v_j$ of $C_4$: the position $(2, 0, 0, 1)$ lies in
$Y_{aabc}$, the position $(0, 1, 0, 0)$ lies in $\hat Y_{abac}$, the position $(0, 0, 0, 0)$ lies
in $\hat Y_{abab}$, and the position $(1, 1, 0, 0)$ lies in $(\hat Y_{abab})^c$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definitions of the sets `Y`).

articles.title: The set $X_{aaab}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $X_{aaab}$ when there is an index $i$ such that
$a_i \equiv a_{i+1} \equiv a_{i+2} \pmod 3$ and $a_{i-1} \not\equiv a_i \pmod 3$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `X_{aaab}`).

articles.title: The set $\hat X_{aabb}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $\hat X_{aabb}$ when there is $i \in \{0, 1\}$ with
$a_i \equiv a_{i+1} \pmod 3$ and $a_{i+2} \equiv a_{i-1} \pmod 3$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `\hat X_{aabb}`).

articles.title: The set $X_{aabc}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $X_{aabc}$ when there is an index $i$ with $a_i \equiv a_{i+1} \pmod 3$ such
that $a_i$, $a_{i+2}$ and $a_{i-1}$ are pairwise incongruent modulo $3$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `X_{aabc}`).

articles.title: The set $X_{abab}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$ lies in $X_{abab}$
when $a_0 \equiv a_2 \pmod 3$, $a_1 \equiv a_3 \pmod 3$ and $a_0 \not\equiv a_1 \pmod 3$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `X_{abab}`).

articles.title: The set $X_{abac}$ of $C_4$ positions
articles.statement:
A position $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of
natural-number pebble counts on the vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$, with indices read
modulo $4$, lies in $X_{abac}$ when there is $i \in \{0, 1\}$ with $a_i \equiv a_{i+2} \pmod 3$
such that $a_i$, $a_{i+1}$ and $a_{i-1}$ are pairwise incongruent modulo $3$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definition of `X_{abac}`).

articles.title: Closure of the mod-$3$ pattern classes under moves on $C_4$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be
distributions of pebbles on the vertices of the $4$-cycle $C_4$ such that $b$ is obtained from $a$
by one $(2:1)$-pebbling move, that is, by removing two pebbles from a vertex holding at least two
pebbles and adding one pebble to an adjacent vertex. If $a \in \hat X_{aabb} \cup X_{abac}$, then
$b \in \hat X_{aabb} \cup X_{abac}$; and if $a \in X_{aaab} \cup X_{abab} \cup X_{aabc}$, then
$b \in X_{aaab} \cup X_{abab} \cup X_{aabc}$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Lemma 15.

articles.title: Examples of the mod-$3$ pattern classes on $C_4$
articles.statement:
Writing a distribution of pebbles on the
vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$ of $C_4$ as $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$, we have
$(0,0,0,0) \in \hat X_{aabb}$, $(1,0,0,0) \in X_{aaab}$, $(0,1,0,1) \in X_{abab}$,
$(0,0,1,2) \in X_{aabc}$, $(0,1,0,2) \in X_{abac}$, and $(0,0,0,0) \notin X_{aaab}$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Section 3 (definitions of the sets `X`).

articles.title: Invariance of the mod-$3$ pattern classes under symmetric replies on $C_4$
articles.statement:
Consider the
$(2:1)$-pebbling game on the cycle $C_4$ with vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3$, indices read modulo
$4$, and let $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ be a position with $a_i$ pebbles on $v_i$. Let $j$ be an
index with $a_j \ge 2$, let $\varepsilon \in \{1, -1\}$, and let $b$ be the position obtained from
$a$ by the move from $v_j$ to $v_{j+\varepsilon}$, which removes two pebbles from $v_j$ and adds
one pebble to $v_{j+\varepsilon}$. Let $c$ be obtained from $b$ either by the move from $v_{j+2}$
to $v_{j-\varepsilon}$, where $b_{j+2} \ge 2$, or by the move from $v_{j-\varepsilon}$ to
$v_{j+2}$, where $b_{j-\varepsilon} \ge 2$. Then for each of the sets $X_{aaab}$, $X_{abab}$,
$X_{aabc}$, $X_{abac}$ and $\hat X_{aabb}$, if $a$ lies in the set, then so does $c$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Lemma 14.

articles.title: All-N threshold of $(2:1)$-pebbling on $K_n$ for even $n$
articles.statement:
For every even $n \ge 6$, the
least number $m$ such that every $(2:1)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_n$ with $m$
pebbles in total is an N-game, written $m^{(2:1)}(K_n)$, exists and equals $n + 7$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Theorem 1(e), quoting Fiorini, Lind, Woldar, and Wong (2021).

articles.title: All-N threshold of $(2:1)$-pebbling on $K_4$
articles.statement:
The least number $m$ such that every
$(2:1)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_4$ with $m$ pebbles in total is an N-game, written
$m^{(2:1)}(K_4)$, exists and equals $23$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Theorem 1(c), quoting Fiorini, Lind, Woldar, and Wong (2021).

articles.title: All-N threshold of $(2:1)$-pebbling on $K_n$ for odd $n$
articles.statement:
For every odd $n \ge 5$, the
least number $m$ such that every $(2:1)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_n$ with $m$
pebbles in total is an N-game, written $m^{(2:1)}(K_n)$, exists and equals $n + 2$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Theorem 1(d), quoting Fiorini, Lind, Woldar, and Wong (2021).

articles.title: All-N threshold of $(k+1:k)$-pebbling on $K_3$
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $k$, the least
number $m$ such that every $(k+1:k)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_3$ with $m$ pebbles in
total is an N-game, written $m^{(k+1:k)}(K_3)$, exists and equals $6k + 1$.

## Sources

- Barker, DeStefano, Fiorini, Gohn, Miller, Roeder, and Wong, *Generalized Impartial Two-player Pebbling Games on `K_3` and `C_4`*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.8, Theorem 2.

articles.title: All-N threshold of $(2:1)$-pebbling on $K_3$
articles.statement:
The least number $m$ such that every
$(2:1)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_3$ with $m$ pebbles in total is an N-game, written
$m^{(2:1)}(K_3)$, exists and equals $7$.

## Sources
